DeMarco, Commissioner of the Environment and Sustainable Development, appeared before the committee to discuss audit work on climate change alongside Kimberly Leach and Elsa Da Costa. He reported that Canada has failed to meet any greenhouse gas emission reduction targets set since 1990. While 2022 national emissions represent a 7% decrease from 2005 levels, they remain 16% higher than 1990 levels. Current projections indicate existing measures will not be sufficient to meet the 2030 commitment of reducing emissions by 40% to 45% below 2005 levels. Mr. DeMarco noted that at the time of his 2021 report, then-current measures were expected to yield only a 36% reduction by 2030. He highlighted that the electricity sector is leading reductions. He recommended the government take stock of existing policies and noted his November 2021 report, which identifies eight lessons learned. He also referenced Environment and Climate Change Canada's 2023 report under the Canadian Net-Zero Emissions Accountability Act, which confirms a remaining gap between current actions and the 2030 target. He concluded by emphasizing that diligent implementation of this Act is necessary to establish the accountability and oversight framework required to achieve future targets. Since 2021, the office has reviewed approximately 40 of the more than 140 measures outlined in the 2030 Emissions Reduction Plan.

He reported that Canada has failed to meet any greenhouse gas emission reduction targets set since 1990. Current projections indicate existing measures will not be sufficient to meet the 2030 commitment of reducing emissions by 40% to 45% below 2005 levels. Mr. DeMarco highlighted that the electricity sector is leading reductions and noted that since 2021, his office has reviewed approximately 40 of the 140+ measures in the 2030 Emissions Reduction Plan. A November 2024 report identified systemic issues including implementation delays and unreliable estimates. The Commissioner emphasized that experts and international organizations agree on the necessity of a policy mix including regulations and carbon pricing. He noted that for these measures to be effective, they must be sufficiently stringent and applied on a large scale. He concluded that diligent implementation of the Canadian Net-Zero Emissions Accountability Act is essential for establishing the required oversight framework.

queries.query_text: Canadian Net-Zero Emissions Accountability Act oversight framework requirements
queries.hypothetical_response: The Canadian Net-Zero Emissions Accountability Act (S.C. 2021, c. 22) mandates the establishment of national emissions reduction targets for 2030, 2035, 2040, and 2045, with a final goal of net-zero by 2050. It requires the Minister of Environment to table an emissions reduction plan, a progress report, and an assessment report for each target. The Act also establishes the Net-Zero Advisory Body to provide independent advice and requires the Commissioner of the Environment and Sustainable Development to examine and report on the government's implementation of measures at least once every five years.

DeMarco, Commissioner of the Environment and Sustainable Development, appeared before the committee to discuss audit work on climate change, specifically the 2030 Emissions Reduction Plan and the $8-billion Net Zero Accelerator (NZA) fund. The Commissioner expressed concern over this discrepancy, noting a lack of transparency and evidence regarding the additional 13 to 14 megatonnes. Conservative MP Dan Mazier raised further concerns, alleging that the government is refusing to disclose the specific emission reduction target for the $8-billion NZA fund to the public, citing that information may be protected under cabinet confidence.

data.meeting_summary: Jerry V. DeMarco, Commissioner of the Environment and Sustainable Development, appeared before the committee to discuss audit work on climate change, specifically the 2030 Emissions Reduction Plan and the $8-billion Net Zero Accelerator (NZA) fund. He reported that Canada has historically failed to meet greenhouse gas emission reduction targets since 1990, and current measures are deemed insufficient for the 2030 goal of a 40% to 45% reduction. A November 2024 report highlighted systemic issues such as implementation delays and unreliable estimates. During questioning, the Commissioner emphasized a significant gap regarding the NZA: while his audit found just over six megatonnes of reductions, the department claims 19 to 20 megatonnes. Conservative MP Dan Mazier raised concerns regarding the use of cabinet confidence to protect specific emission reduction targets and oil/gas figures from public disclosure, noting that this obscures value-for-money calculations. Specifically, Mazier highlighted a $700-million allocation from the NZA fund to PowerCo, pointing out that the industry department was unable to provide the committee with specific emission reduction figures. The Commissioner noted that the most significant concerns regarding inaccurate emission estimates are concentrated within grants and contributions related to Pillar One of the NZA, asserting that if such significant funds are disbursed, there should be an estimation of the benefits.

data.meeting_summary: Jerry V. DeMarco, Commissioner of the Environment and Sustainable Development, discussed audit work on the 2030 Emissions Reduction Plan and the $8-billion Net Zero Accelerator (NZA) fund. He noted Canada's historical failure to meet greenhouse gas targets since 1990 and indicated that current measures are insufficient for the 2030 goal of a 40% to 45% reduction. A November 2024 report highlighted systemic issues including implementation delays and unreliable estimates. The Commissioner noted a significant data gap: his audit found six megatonnes of reductions while the department claimed 19 to 20 megatonnes. Conservative MP Dan Mazier raised concerns regarding the use of cabinet confidence to shield specific emission targets from public disclosure, specifically citing a $700-million allocation to PowerCo where the industry department could not provide reduction figures. MP Dan Mazier further noted that the environment committee ordered the government to hand over all contracts related to the $8-billion NZA fund, but alleged that the government redacted over 360 pages. The Commissioner clarified that while he cannot speak for the committee's access, his office has "free access" provisions in their legislation that allow them to see such documents, advocating for publication of the value reaped from public subsidies rather than a "just trust us" approach.

queries.query_text: parliamentary rules for redaction of sensitive information in committee documents
queries.hypothetical_response: The House of Commons Procedure and Practice notes that while committees have the power to order the production of documents, the government may redact information based on cabinet confidence, national security, or personal privacy. However, committees often contest these redactions, asserting their 'absolute' right to unfettered access to information required for their studies.

queries.query_text: Net Zero Accelerator Pillar One emission reduction targets and reporting requirements
queries.hypothetical_response: Pillar One of the Net Zero Accelerator focuses on Decarbonization of Large Emitters. Documents typically outline specific megatonne (Mt) CO2e reduction targets per project. Public reporting usually includes aggregate figures, but facility-specific data is often protected under commercial confidentiality clauses in contribution agreements.

queries.query_text: Auditor General access to unredacted government contracts and cabinet confidences
queries.hypothetical_response: Under the Auditor General Act, the AG has a legal right to access almost all government records necessary for an audit, including many documents protected by solicitor-client privilege or commercial confidentiality. However, Section 39 of the Canada Evidence Act regarding Cabinet confidences remains a primary barrier to full access for the AG's office.

He highlighted that current measures are insufficient for the 2030 goal, noting a discrepancy where his audit found 6 megatonnes of reductions versus the 19-20 megatonnes claimed by the department. Conservative MP Dan Mazier raised concerns regarding over 360 redacted pages in NZA contracts. The Commissioner clarified that while he has legislative access to documents, he shares concerns regarding the lack of public transparency. Liberal MP Leah Taylor Roy shifted the discussion to the "lessons learned" section of the Commissioner's report, specifically Lesson 2. She noted the Commissioner's observation that no Canadian government since 1990 has successfully met its emission reduction targets, highlighting a historical failure across different governing parties. Ms. Taylor Roy further explored the structural challenges identified in the report, specifically how the Canadian economy's dependence on emission-intensive sectors like oil and gas contributes to these repeated failures. She is currently questioning the Commissioner on potential levers and strategies to ensure the oil and gas sector meets future targets.

data.meeting_summary: Jerry V. DeMarco, Commissioner of the Environment and Sustainable Development, discussed audit findings on the 2030 Emissions Reduction Plan and the $8-billion Net Zero Accelerator (NZA) fund. He noted a 13-14 megatonne discrepancy in claimed versus audited reductions and emphasized that managing oil, gas, and transportation is essential to meeting national targets. MP Dan Mazier raised concerns regarding over 360 redacted pages in NZA contracts, while MP Leah Taylor Roy noted these contracts contain qualitative descriptions of reduction methods. Rhéal Fortin (Bloc Québécois) challenged the Commissioner on Report 7 findings, noting that no new substantive federal measures have been included in emissions modelling since 2022. The Commissioner confirmed that current measures are insufficient, projecting only a 36% reduction against the minimum 40% target. He expressed disappointment that three years after identifying this 4% gap in 2021 (Report 5), the deficit remains. While MP Fortin pressed for specific policy recommendations to bridge the gap, the Commissioner clarified that the Office of the Auditor General's mandate is restricted to assessing performance and value for money, rather than selecting or prescribing specific government policies.

data.meeting_summary: Jerry V. DeMarco, Commissioner of the Environment and Sustainable Development, discussed audit findings on the 2030 Emissions Reduction Plan and the $8-billion Net Zero Accelerator fund. He noted a 13-14 megatonne discrepancy, projecting a 36% reduction against the 40% target based on ECCC data. The Commissioner clarified that while his office believes the actual reduction will be lower than 36% due to overestimations and double counting, they have not produced a specific competing numerical estimate as only 40 of 140+ measures were reviewed. He expressed frustration that the projection remains at 36%, unchanged since 2021. The Commissioner argues the government must first provide a plan that mathematically meets the 40-45% target on paper before his office can effectively audit the validity of those projections. Laurel Collins (NDP) raised concerns regarding the influence of the oil and gas sector and requested specific policy areas needing increased stringency. The Commissioner identified weaknesses in carbon pricing, specifically regarding the fairness and balance between industrial pricing and consumer/retail pricing, particularly highlighting impacts on small businesses and indigenous peoples.

data.meeting_summary: Jerry V. DeMarco, Commissioner of the Environment and Sustainable Development, discussed audit findings on the 2030 Emissions Reduction Plan and the $8-billion Net Zero Accelerator fund. He noted a 13-14 megatonne discrepancy, projecting a 36% reduction against the 40% target. The Commissioner stated that the government must provide a plan that mathematically meets the 40-45% target on paper before its validity can be fully audited. While the Commissioner identified weaknesses in carbon pricing fairness for small businesses and indigenous peoples, he noted that increasing stringency in regulations or pricing is a government policy choice. Laurel Collins (NDP) questioned the necessity of an emissions cap given industry claims. She highlighted that major oil and gas companies like Suncor, Imperial Oil, and Shell Canada testified that an emissions cap was unnecessary because they had internal targets, though she emphasized these targets are not legally binding. The Commissioner acknowledged that while voluntary emissions reductions are technically possible, the track record for such measures remains a critical factor. He noted that despite improvements in emissions intensity—where the oil and gas sector increases the efficiency with which it pollutes—overall emissions have not decreased because intensity benefits have been outweighed by larger increases in production. He committed to providing the committee with a graph illustrating greenhouse gas emissions by sector from 1990 to the present.

DeMarco, Commissioner of the Environment and Sustainable Development, discussed audit findings on the 2030 Emissions Reduction Plan and the $8-billion Net Zero Accelerator fund. He noted a 13-14 megatonne discrepancy, projecting a 36% reduction against the 40% target. The Commissioner stated that the government must provide a plan that mathematically meets the 40-45% target on paper before its validity can be fully audited. While the Commissioner identified weaknesses in carbon pricing fairness for small businesses and indigenous peoples, he noted that increasing stringency is a policy choice. Laurel Collins (NDP) questioned the necessity of an emissions cap given that oil and gas companies testified their internal targets make a cap unnecessary, though these are not legally binding. The Commissioner acknowledged that while voluntary reductions are possible, the track record is a concern. He noted that despite improvements in emissions intensity, overall emissions in the oil and gas sector have not decreased because efficiency gains were outweighed by production increases. Gérard Deltell (Conservative) emphasized the need for results and fiscal responsibility regarding the $8-billion Net-Zero Accelerator initiative, noting the funds come from taxpayers and specifically mentioning that GST revenues are used to pay interest on the national debt.

DeMarco, Commissioner of the Environment and Sustainable Development, discussed audit findings on the 2030 Emissions Reduction Plan and the $8-billion Net Zero Accelerator fund. The Commissioner stated that the government must provide a plan that mathematically meets the 40-45% target on paper before its validity can be fully audited. While the Commissioner identified weaknesses in carbon pricing fairness for small businesses and indigenous peoples, he noted that increasing stringency is a policy choice. Laurel Collins (NDP) questioned the necessity of an emissions cap given oil and gas companies' non-binding internal targets. The Commissioner noted that despite improvements in emissions intensity, overall emissions in the oil and gas sector have not decreased because efficiency gains were outweighed by production increases. Gérard Deltell (Conservative) questioned the effectiveness and fiscal responsibility of the $8-billion Net-Zero Accelerator. The Commissioner highlighted significant concerns, including a lack of transparency in value for money and a lack of horizontal policy for the sector. He revealed that only five agreements have been signed with companies receiving funding to reduce greenhouse gas emissions through this initiative.

DeMarco, Commissioner of the Environment and Sustainable Development, discussed audit findings on the 2030 Emissions Reduction Plan and the $8-billion Net Zero Accelerator fund. He noted a 13-14 megatonne discrepancy, projecting a 36% reduction against the 40% target. The Commissioner emphasized that transparency is essential for both officers of Parliament and the committee to assess government progress. While identified weaknesses in carbon pricing fairness exist, he noted stringency is a policy choice. Laurel Collins (NDP) questioned the necessity of an emissions cap given oil and gas production increases. Gérard Deltell (Conservative) criticized the Net-Zero Accelerator for a lack of transparency and horizontal policy, noting only five signed agreements. Specific concern was raised regarding a $700 million grant to a foreign firm for an Ontario plant that reportedly lacks specific emission reduction targets. The Commissioner confirmed his report shares these concerns regarding value for money, stating the department must justify these expenditures. He reiterated that improved transparency would build public confidence in climate action by demonstrating that taxpayer money is being used effectively to achieve measurable results.

Discussions highlighted transparency concerns regarding 360 pages of redacted documents. Sophie Chatel (Liberal) cited a Canadian Climate Institute analysis identifying industrial carbon pricing as the primary driver for emission reductions, supported by 300 economists. The meeting addressed political friction regarding the potential abolition of federal carbon pricing. Ms. Chatel argued that because the federal tax does not apply to Quebec, its abolition elsewhere would leave Quebec isolated. The Commissioner emphasized that the federal carbon price accounts for approximately 30% of total emissions reductions; consequently, if abolished, a measure of equal or greater restrictiveness would be required to maintain progress. He identified the primary tools for reduction as pricing, regulations, subsidies, and education. The Commissioner clarified that replacing pricing with regulation would require creating an entirely new regime, essentially forcing the government to "start from scratch" and potentially stalling progress toward the 36% to 40% reduction target.

data.meeting_summary: Jerry V. DeMarco, Commissioner of the Environment and Sustainable Development, discussed audit findings on the 2030 Emissions Reduction Plan and the $8-billion Net Zero Accelerator fund. Discussions highlighted transparency concerns regarding 360 pages of redacted documents. Sophie Chatel (Liberal) cited analysis identifying industrial carbon pricing as the primary driver for emission reductions, supported by 300 economists. The meeting addressed political friction regarding the potential abolition of federal carbon pricing. Ms. Chatel argued that because the federal tax does not apply to Quebec, its abolition elsewhere would leave Quebec isolated. The Commissioner emphasized that the federal carbon price accounts for approximately 30% of total emissions reductions; consequently, if abolished, a measure of equal or greater restrictiveness would be required to maintain progress. He identified the primary tools for reduction as pricing, regulations, subsidies, and education. The Commissioner clarified that replacing pricing with regulation would require creating an entirely new regime, essentially forcing the government to "start from scratch". Ms. Chatel outlined three hypothetical scenarios following abolition: the first being a "do nothing" approach where emissions increase and Quebec is isolated; the second being a prescriptive regulatory approach setting specific emission thresholds; and the third being a strategy of massive investments which would increase public debt. The Commissioner noted that relying on grants and subsidies is not only expensive but has historically failed to yield major emission reductions according to recent reports.

DeMarco, Commissioner of the Environment and Sustainable Development, discussed audit findings on the 2030 Emissions Reduction Plan and the $8-billion Net Zero Accelerator fund. Discussions highlighted transparency concerns regarding 360 pages of redacted documents. Sophie Chatel (Liberal) cited analysis identifying industrial carbon pricing as the primary driver for emission reductions, supported by 300 economists. The meeting addressed political friction regarding the potential abolition of federal carbon pricing. The Commissioner emphasized that the federal carbon price accounts for approximately 30% of total emissions reductions; consequently, if abolished, a measure of equal or greater restrictiveness would be required to maintain progress. He identified the primary tools for reduction as pricing, regulations, subsidies, and education. The Commissioner clarified that replacing pricing with regulation would require creating an entirely new regime, essentially forcing the government to "start from scratch". Ms. Chatel outlined three hypothetical scenarios following abolition: a "do nothing" approach, a prescriptive regulatory approach setting specific emission thresholds, and a strategy of massive investments which would increase public debt. The Commissioner noted that relying on grants and subsidies is not only expensive but has historically failed to yield major emission reductions. Rhéal Fortin (Bloc Québécois) shifted the inquiry toward international comparisons. The Commissioner clarified that Canada maintains a national carbon pricing system where provinces and territories can implement their own systems or fall under the federal backstop, ensuring a system exists in all jurisdictions.

data.meeting_summary: Jerry V. DeMarco, Commissioner of the Environment and Sustainable Development, discussed audit findings on the 2030 Emissions Reduction Plan and the $8-billion Net Zero Accelerator fund. Discussions highlighted transparency concerns regarding redacted documents and the primary drivers for emission reductions, with industrial carbon pricing identified as a key factor. The Commissioner emphasized that the federal carbon price accounts for approximately 30% of total reductions and warned that replacing pricing with regulation would force the government to "start from scratch." Ms. Chatel (Liberal) outlined three hypothetical scenarios following the abolition of pricing: a "do nothing" approach, a prescriptive regulatory approach, and a strategy of massive investments increasing public debt. Rhéal Fortin (Bloc Québécois) questioned the effectiveness of Canada's system compared to international models. The Commissioner clarified that Canada's national pricing system, which allows for provincial flexibility, is similar to the European Union's cap-and-trade system. However, the Commissioner noted that while he has not conducted a direct comparative analysis between Canada and G20 countries, Canada currently holds the worst emissions record in the G7 since 1990. He further clarified that carbon pricing is a relatively recent measure compared to the long-term data being tracked.
